title: Systematic improvement of user engagement with academic titles using computational linguistics
venue: Proceedings of the Informing Science and Information Technology Education Conference
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the wording of digital content can systematically influence user engagement, and whether computational linguistics can be used to create more engaging text. The authors frame the work around user engagement theory, cumulative prospect theory, and digital nudging, proposing that certain words with high familiarity, novelty, or emotionality can improve how information is selected and evaluated.

To test this, the authors ran a pilot study on academic titles. They built a computational pipeline using JSTOR academic titles, IMDB keywords, TF-IDF, sentiment analysis, and lexical/semantic substitution to produce modified titles containing “sticky words.” Participants were undergraduate students at a large U.S. research university. Using a between-group randomized A/B design in Qualtrics, participants saw either original or modified titles and then indicated whether they would read them and completed User Engagement Scale items.

The results showed that modified titles were selected more often and received higher engagement/evaluation scores than original titles. The authors conclude that wording alone can meaningfully shape information interactions and that computational linguistics offers a systematic way to evaluate and optimize digital content. They present the study as an early proof of concept and note that the model still needs refinement and testing in other contexts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed pilot experimental study with a between-group design, but it is not a K-12 education study and does not evaluate Khanmigo or science outcomes. It provides a small, context-specific engagement finding rather than rigorous evidence for the target intervention/topic.
impact_tier_rationale: The study does not address K-12 science learning or Khanmigo, and its outcomes are limited to title selection and perceived engagement in a university sample. Its relevance to the requested evidence question is therefore negligible.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot A/B test with n=216 undergraduate participants, titles modified with 'sticky words' produced significantly higher user engagement and selection to read the article than original titles. Selection increased from M=.51 (SD=.503) to M=.78 (SD=.414), t(214)=4.423, p<.001, and evaluation using the User Engagement Scale increased from M=3.21 (SD=1.11) to M=3.86 (SD=.80), t(214)=5.031, p<.001.
finding.measure: User Engagement Scale ratings and binary selection-to-read behavior
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for UES mean difference [-0.90702, -0.39637]; selection CI not_reported
finding.std_deviation: original UES SD=1.10530; treatment UES SD=0.79795
